claim: Fast Ca2+-triggered vesicle fusion with reconstituted neuronal SNAREs and synaptotagmin-1 begins from an initial hemifusion-free membrane point contact, rather than a hemifusion diaphragm.
source: Previously we showed that fast Ca2+-triggered vesicle fusion with reconstituted neuronal SNAREs and synaptotagmin-1 begins from an initial hemifusion-free membrane point contact, rather than a hemifusion diaphragm, using a single vesicle–vesicle lipid/content mixing assay (Diao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Diao et al., 2012) that used a single vesicle-vesicle assay.

claim: When complexin-1 was included, a more pronounced Ca2+-triggered fusion burst was observed, effectively synchronizing the process.
source: When complexin-1 was included, a more pronounced Ca2+-triggered fusion burst was observed, effectively synchronizing the process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Diao et al., 2012) mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Complexin-1 reduces spontaneous fusion in the single vesicle-vesicle assay.
source: Here we show that complexin-1 also reduces spontaneous fusion in the same assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 2B showing reduced spontaneous fusion with complexin-1.

claim: Distinct effects of several complexin-1 truncation mutants on spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion closely mimic those observed in neuronal cultures.
source: Moreover, distinct effects of several complexin-1 truncation mutants on spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion closely mimic those observed in neuronal cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and comparison to cited neuronal culture studies.

claim: The very N-terminal domain is essential for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion, but not for suppression of spontaneous fusion.
source: The very N-terminal domain is essential for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion, but not for suppression of spontaneous fusion, whereas the opposite is true for the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G comparing different complexin-1 truncation mutants.

claim: The C-terminal domain is essential for suppression of spontaneous fusion, but not for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion.
source: The very N-terminal domain is essential for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion, but not for suppression of spontaneous fusion, whereas the opposite is true for the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G comparing different complexin-1 truncation mutants.

claim: Differences in titration behavior for spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion were observed by systematically varying the complexin-1 concentration.
source: By systematically varying the complexin-1 concentration, we observed differences in titration behavior for spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 showing concentration-dependent effects.

claim: Complexin-1 utilizes distinct mechanisms for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion and inhibition of spontaneous fusion.
source: Taken together, complexin-1 utilizes distinct mechanisms for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion and inhibition of spontaneous fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental observations of differential domain requirements and titration behaviors.

claim: Neuronal SNAREs provide the minimal energy to drive membrane fusion.
source: While it is well established that SNARE proteins provide the minimal energy to drive membrane fusion (Weber et al., 1998) and synaptotagmin-1 is the Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous release (Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001), the molecular mechanisms of complexin, Munc18, and Munc13 are less certain (Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weber et al., 1998.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 is the Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous release.
source: While it is well established that SNARE proteins provide the minimal energy to drive membrane fusion (Weber et al., 1998) and synaptotagmin-1 is the Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous release (Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001), the molecular mechanisms of complexin, Munc18, and Munc13 are less certain (Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of complexin, Munc18, and Munc13 are less certain.
source: While it is well established that SNARE proteins provide the minimal energy to drive membrane fusion (Weber et al., 1998) and synaptotagmin-1 is the Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous release (Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001), the molecular mechanisms of complexin, Munc18, and Munc13 are less certain (Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).

claim: Complexin is a small soluble protein of 134 residues found mainly in the presynaptic terminal.
source: Complexin is a small soluble protein of 134 residues found mainly in the presynaptic terminal.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about complexin.

claim: Studies in cortical neuronal cultures revealed that complexin 'activates' fast synchronous release and inhibits spontaneous 'mini' release.
source: Studies in cortical neuronal cultures revealed that complexin 'activates' fast synchronous release and inhibits spontaneous 'mini' release (Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012); these studies used RNA-interference double-knockdown of both complexin-1 and complexin-2 isoforms combined with rescue by various truncation and point mutants of complexin-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maximov et al., 2009 and Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012.

claim: Complexin double-knockout mice showed impairment of both synchronous and spontaneous release in hippocampal neurons.
source: In contrast, complexin double-knockout mice showed impairment of both synchronous and spontaneous release in hippocampal neurons (Reim et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reim et al., 2001 and Xue et al., 2010.

claim: A complexin double-knockout in Drosophila impaired synchronous release but enhanced spontaneous release.
source: At variance, a complexin double-knockout in Drosophila impaired synchronous release but enhanced spontaneous release (Xue et al., 2009; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xue et al., 2009 and Jorquera et al., 2012.

claim: Overexpression of complexin-1 in PC12 cells suppressed both K+-dependent acetylcholine release.
source: Overexpression of complexin-1 in PC12 cells suppressed both K+-dependent acetylcholine release (Itakura et al., 1999) and evoked release in chromaffin cells (Archer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Itakura et al., 1999.

claim: Overexpression of complexin-1 in PC12 cells suppressed evoked release in chromaffin cells.
source: Overexpression of complexin-1 in PC12 cells suppressed both K+-dependent acetylcholine release (Itakura et al., 1999) and evoked release in chromaffin cells (Archer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Archer et al., 2002.

claim: Expressing synaptobrevin-fused complexin-1 in cultured cortical neurons substantially diminished both spontaneous and evoked neurotransmitter release.
source: Moreover, expressing synaptobrevin-fused complexin-1 in cultured cortical neurons substantially diminished both spontaneous and evoked neurotransmitter release (Tang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2006.

claim: A consensus has emerged that the two main physiological functions of complexin in neurons at normal expression levels consist of activation of synchronous release and suppression of spontaneous release.
source: Taken together, a consensus has emerged that the two main physiological functions of complexin in neurons at normal expression levels consist of activation of synchronous release and suppression of spontaneous release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the body of literature cited in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The N-terminal domain (residues 1–27) of complexin-1 activates fast synchronous release.
source: The N-terminal domain (residues 1–27) of complexin-1 activates fast synchronous release whereas the accessory helix domain (residues 28–48) is critical for suppressing spontaneous release (Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maximov et al., 2009.

claim: The accessory helix domain (residues 28–48) is critical for suppressing spontaneous release.
source: The N-terminal domain (residues 1–27) of complexin-1 activates fast synchronous release whereas the accessory helix domain (residues 28–48) is critical for suppressing spontaneous release (Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maximov et al., 2009.

claim: The α-helical SNARE binding domain of complexin-1 (residues 49–70) is essential for all physiological functions.
source: The α-helical SNARE binding domain of complexin-1 (residues 49–70) is essential for all physiological functions; it binds to the groove between the synaptobrevin-2 and syntaxin-1A α-helices in the core part of the neuronal SNARE complex (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2002.

claim: The SNARE binding domain of complexin-1 binds to the groove between the synaptobrevin-2 and syntaxin-1A α-helices in the core part of the neuronal SNARE complex.
source: The α-helical SNARE binding domain of complexin-1 (residues 49–70) is essential for all physiological functions; it binds to the groove between the synaptobrevin-2 and syntaxin-1A α-helices in the core part of the neuronal SNARE complex (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2002.

claim: The C-terminal domain (residues 71–134) has a role in suppressing spontaneous release.
source: The C-terminal domain (residues 71–134) has a role in suppressing spontaneous release, but it is expendable for evoked release (Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012.

claim: The C-terminal domain is expendable for evoked release.
source: The C-terminal domain (residues 71–134) has a role in suppressing spontaneous release, but it is expendable for evoked release (Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012.

claim: The C-terminal domain promotes vesicle priming.
source: The C-terminal domain also promotes vesicle priming (Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012) and binding to anionic membranes (Diao et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012.

claim: The C-terminal domain binds to anionic membranes.
source: The C-terminal domain also promotes vesicle priming (Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012) and binding to anionic membranes (Diao et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diao et al., 2013b.

claim: The presence of complexin-1 greatly enhances the burst of fusion events upon Ca2+-injection.
source: Previously, we used a single vesicle–vesicle lipid/content mixing assay with reconstituted neuronal SNAREs, synaptotagmin-1, and complexin-1 to decipher the membrane states upon Ca2+-triggering, and we found that the presence of complexin-1 greatly enhances the burst of fusion events upon Ca2+-injection, that is, complexin-1 effectively synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion in our minimal system (Diao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Diao et al., 2012).

claim: Complexin-1 effectively synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion in the minimal reconstituted system.
source: Previously, we used a single vesicle–vesicle lipid/content mixing assay with reconstituted neuronal SNAREs, synaptotagmin-1, and complexin-1 to decipher the membrane states upon Ca2+-triggering, and we found that the presence of complexin-1 greatly enhances the burst of fusion events upon Ca2+-injection, that is, complexin-1 effectively synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion in our minimal system (Diao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Diao et al., 2012).

claim: The probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection with complexin-1 is 1.7%.
source: As before, we observed that complexin-1 synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion together with synaptotagmin-1 and neuronal SNAREs, producing a higher amplitude upon Ca2+ triggering (the probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection with and without complexin-1 is 1.7% and 0.6%, respectively) and a faster decay rate (with complexin-1: 0.43 s−1, without complexin-1: 0.11 s−1) (Figure 2A), in qualitative agreement with studies of cultured cortical mouse neurons and in Drosophila (Reim et al., 2001; Maximov et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection without complexin-1 is 0.6%.
source: As before, we observed that complexin-1 synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion together with synaptotagmin-1 and neuronal SNAREs, producing a higher amplitude upon Ca2+ triggering (the probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection with and without complexin-1 is 1.7% and 0.6%, respectively) and a faster decay rate (with complexin-1: 0.43 s−1, without complexin-1: 0.11 s−1) (Figure 2A), in qualitative agreement with studies of cultured cortical mouse neurons and in Drosophila (Reim et al., 2001; Maximov et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decay rate of Ca2+-triggered fusion with complexin-1 is 0.43 s−1.
source: As before, we observed that complexin-1 synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion together with synaptotagmin-1 and neuronal SNAREs, producing a higher amplitude upon Ca2+ triggering (the probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection with and without complexin-1 is 1.7% and 0.6%, respectively) and a faster decay rate (with complexin-1: 0.43 s−1, without complexin-1: 0.11 s−1) (Figure 2A), in qualitative agreement with studies of cultured cortical mouse neurons and in Drosophila (Reim et al., 2001; Maximov et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decay rate of Ca2+-triggered fusion without complexin-1 is 0.11 s−1.
source: As before, we observed that complexin-1 synchronizes Ca2+-triggered fusion together with synaptotagmin-1 and neuronal SNAREs, producing a higher amplitude upon Ca2+ triggering (the probability of fusion per associated vesicle in the first 1-sec time bin upon Ca2+-injection with and without complexin-1 is 1.7% and 0.6%, respectively) and a faster decay rate (with complexin-1: 0.43 s−1, without complexin-1: 0.11 s−1) (Figure 2A), in qualitative agreement with studies of cultured cortical mouse neurons and in Drosophila (Reim et al., 2001; Maximov et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2010; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The probability of spontaneous fusion per associated vesicle with complexin-1 is 0.02% per sec.
source: With our improved assay, we also observed that complexin-1 suppresses spontaneous fusion (Figure 2B) (the probability of spontaneous fusion per associated vesicle with and without complexin-1 is 0.02% and 0.1% per sec, respectively), in qualitative agreement with knockdown studies in cortical neuronal cultures (Maximov et al., 2009), as well as knockout studies in Drosophila (Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The probability of spontaneous fusion per associated vesicle without complexin-1 is 0.1% per sec.
source: With our improved assay, we also observed that complexin-1 suppresses spontaneous fusion (Figure 2B) (the probability of spontaneous fusion per associated vesicle with and without complexin-1 is 0.02% and 0.1% per sec, respectively), in qualitative agreement with knockdown studies in cortical neuronal cultures (Maximov et al., 2009), as well as knockout studies in Drosophila (Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of complexin-1, the ratio of the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion is 85 times higher than the probability of spontaneous fusion.
source: Thus, in the presence of complexin-1, the ratio of the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion is 85 times higher than the probability of spontaneous fusion, whereas in the absence of complexin this ratio is only 6; so complexin increases this ratio more than ten fold.
evidence: This claim is derived from calculations based on the experimental data presented.

claim: In the absence of complexin-1, the ratio of the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion to spontaneous fusion is only 6.
source: Thus, in the presence of complexin-1, the ratio of the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion is 85 times higher than the probability of spontaneous fusion, whereas in the absence of complexin this ratio is only 6; so complexin increases this ratio more than ten fold.
evidence: This claim is derived from calculations based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Complexin increases the ratio of Ca2+-triggered to spontaneous fusion more than ten fold.
source: Thus, in the presence of complexin-1, the ratio of the probability of Ca2+-triggered fusion is 85 times higher than the probability of spontaneous fusion, whereas in the absence of complexin this ratio is only 6; so complexin increases this ratio more than ten fold.
evidence: This claim is derived from calculations based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The central SNARE-binding domain of complexin-1 is essential for both spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion.
source: We found that the central SNARE-binding domain of complexin-1 is essential for both spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered fusion since mutation of four residues in that domain (R48A, R59A, K69A, Y70A, C105A, termed '4M' mutant [Maximov et al., 2009]) is similar to the control without complexin-1 (compare first and last columns in Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G comparing the 4M mutant to controls.

claim: The N-terminal domain is essential for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion, but not for the suppression of spontaneous fusion.
source: The N-terminal domain is essential for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion, but not for the suppression of spontaneous fusion (third columns in Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G for the Cpx26-134 mutant.

claim: The C-terminal domain is essential for suppressing spontaneous fusion, but not for synchronization.
source: The opposite is true for the C-terminal domain: it is essential for suppressing spontaneous fusion, but not for synchronization (fifth columns in Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G for the Cpx1-86 mutant.

claim: The accessory domain is essential for the suppression of spontaneous fusion.
source: Moreover, the accessory domain is essential for the suppression of spontaneous fusion (fourth columns in Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-G for the Cpx41-134 mutant.

claim: All results with complexin-1 mutants are in excellent qualitative agreement with studies performed with cultured cortical neurons.
source: All these results are in excellent qualitative agreement with studies performed with cultured cortical neurons (Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim compares the experimental results to cited neuronal culture studies.

claim: The suppression of spontaneous fusion by complexin-1 becomes significant between 100 and 500 nM complexin-1.
source: The suppression of spontaneous fusion by complexin-1 becomes significant between 100 and 500 nM complexin-1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of complexin-1 on the synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion becomes significant at lower concentration, between 50 and 100 nM complexin.
source: In contrast, the effect of complexin-1 on the synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion becomes significant at lower concentration, between 50 and 100 nM complexin (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Addition of an excess of the soluble fragment of synaptobrevin-2 (a.a. 1–96) reduced the association between SV and PM vesicles to background levels even at the highest complexin-1 concentration tested (2 μM).
source: As a control, addition of an excess of the soluble fragment of synaptobrevin-2 (a.a. 1–96) reduced the association between SV and PM vesicles to background levels even at the highest complexin-1 concentration tested (2 μM), indicating that complexin-1 alone does not cause significant SV-PM vesicle association (Figure 3A, right-most column).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Complexin-1 alone does not cause significant SV-PM vesicle association.
source: As a control, addition of an excess of the soluble fragment of synaptobrevin-2 (a.a. 1–96) reduced the association between SV and PM vesicles to background levels even at the highest complexin-1 concentration tested (2 μM), indicating that complexin-1 alone does not cause significant SV-PM vesicle association (Figure 3A, right-most column).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the control experiment showing that soluble synaptobrevin blocks association.

claim: The suppression of spontaneous fusion depends only on the presence of complexin-1, but not synaptotagmin-1.
source: We found that the suppression of spontaneous fusion depends only on the presence of complexin-1, but not synaptotagmin-1 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both complexin-1 and synaptotagmin-1 contribute to SV-PM vesicle association (in conjunction with neuronal SNAREs) in an approximately additive fashion.
source: However, both complexin-1 and synaptotagmin-1 contribute to SV-PM vesicle association (in conjunction with neuronal SNAREs) in an approximately additive fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The improved single vesicle–vesicle content-mixing assay mimics characteristics of Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion as well as spontaneous release.
source: Our improved single vesicle–vesicle content-mixing assay mimics characteristics of Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion as well as spontaneous release.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The assay qualitatively reproduces the effects of complexin-1 and key mutations on both spontaneous release and evoked release that have been observed in cortical neuronal cultures.
source: Our assay qualitatively reproduces the effects of complexin-1 and key mutations on both spontaneous release and evoked release that have been observed in cortical neuronal cultures (Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim compares the experimental results to cited neuronal culture studies.

claim: Complexin-1 suppressed SNARE-mediated content-mixing in a cell-based assay.
source: For example, complexin-1 suppressed SNARE-mediated content-mixing in a cell-based assay, and the combination of synaptotagmin-1 and Ca2+ reversed this effect, albeit on a very slow time scale (Giraudo et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giraudo et al., 2009.

claim: The combination of synaptotagmin-1 and Ca2+ reversed the suppression of SNARE-mediated content-mixing by complexin-1, albeit on a very slow time scale.
source: For example, complexin-1 suppressed SNARE-mediated content-mixing in a cell-based assay, and the combination of synaptotagmin-1 and Ca2+ reversed this effect, albeit on a very slow time scale (Giraudo et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giraudo et al., 2009.

claim: Complexin-1 promoted both spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered lipid mixing using a single vesicle–vesicle lipid-mixing assay together with neuronal SNAREs, but in the absence of synaptotagmin-1.
source: Complexin-1 promoted both spontaneous and Ca2+-triggered lipid mixing using a single vesicle–vesicle lipid-mixing assay together with neuronal SNAREs, but, surprisingly, in the absence of synaptotagmin-1 (Yoon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoon et al., 2008.

claim: Complexin-1, together with neuronal SNAREs and synaptotagmin-1, reduced Ca2+-independent lipid-mixing and it enhanced Ca2+-triggered lipid mixing using an ensemble assay.
source: In contrast, complexin-1, together with neuronal SNAREs and synaptotagmin-1, reduced Ca2+-independent lipid-mixing and it enhanced Ca2+-triggered lipid mixing using an ensemble assay (Malsam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Malsam et al., 2012.

claim: An ensemble fluorescence study revealed enhanced lipid-mixing upon Ca2+ triggering with a complexin-1 fragment without the N-terminal and accessory domains.
source: Moreover, this ensemble fluorescence study revealed enhanced lipid-mixing upon Ca2+ triggering with a complexin-1 fragment without the N-terminal and accessory domains.
evidence: This claim refers to the Malsam et al., 2012 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: The lipid-mixing result with complexin-1 fragment does not correlate with the observation that the N-terminus of complexin-1 is essential for activation of fast synchronous release.
source: Thus, this lipid-mixing result does not correlate with the observation that the N-terminus of complexin-1 is essential for activation of fast synchronous release (Figure 1E in Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim compares results from Malsam et al., 2012 to Maximov et al., 2009.

claim: The single vesicle–vesicle content-mixing assay correlates well with the physiological data since the N-terminal and accessory domains are required for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion.
source: In contrast, our single vesicle–vesicle content-mixing assay correlates well with the physiological data since the N-terminal and accessory domains are required for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: Many previous studies suffered from the lack of a genuine content mixing indicator.
source: In retrospect, many previous studies suffered from the lack of a genuine content mixing indicator and the use of an ensemble method that cannot distinguish between effects due to vesicle association and fusion, see discussion in refs. (Diao et al., 2012, 2013c).
evidence: This claim is based on discussion in cited references (Diao et al., 2012, 2013c).

claim: Many previous studies suffered from the use of an ensemble method that cannot distinguish between effects due to vesicle association and fusion.
source: In retrospect, many previous studies suffered from the lack of a genuine content mixing indicator and the use of an ensemble method that cannot distinguish between effects due to vesicle association and fusion, see discussion in refs. (Diao et al., 2012, 2013c).
evidence: This claim is based on discussion in cited references (Diao et al., 2012, 2013c).

claim: The single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay addresses both limitations of previous studies.
source: Our single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay addresses both limitations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the design of the assay and the preceding discussion of limitations.

claim: Another single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay was developed using a much larger probe (dual-labeled DNA hairpin).
source: Another single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay was also developed using a much larger probe (dual-labeled DNA hairpin) (Diao et al., 2010); using this assay, accelerated fusion pore expansion by complexin-1 was observed (Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diao et al., 2010.

claim: Using the DNA hairpin assay, accelerated fusion pore expansion by complexin-1 was observed.
source: Another single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay was also developed using a much larger probe (dual-labeled DNA hairpin) (Diao et al., 2010); using this assay, accelerated fusion pore expansion by complexin-1 was observed (Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lai et al., 2013.

claim: The effect of complexin-1 on synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion becomes significant between 50 and 100 nM, well above the kD of the interaction between complexin-1 and the ternary SNARE complex of ∼10 nM.
source: Our single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay revealed that the effect of complexin-1 on synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion becomes significant between 50 and 100 nM, well above the kD of the interaction between complexin-1 and the ternary SNARE complex of ∼10 nM (Xu et al., 2013), yet the effect on spontaneous fusion becomes only significant at higher complexin concentrations (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and citation to Xu et al., 2013 for the kD value.

claim: The kD of the interaction between complexin-1 and the ternary SNARE complex is ∼10 nM.
source: Our single vesicle–vesicle content mixing assay revealed that the effect of complexin-1 on synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion becomes significant between 50 and 100 nM, well above the kD of the interaction between complexin-1 and the ternary SNARE complex of ∼10 nM (Xu et al., 2013), yet the effect on spontaneous fusion becomes only significant at higher complexin concentrations (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Models of complexin function have primarily focused on a clamping or hindrance mechanism that restricts spontaneous release.
source: Models of complexin function have primarily focused on a clamping or hindrance mechanism that restricts spontaneous release (Giraudo et al., 2006; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Trimbuch et al., 2014), along with a model that combined the clamping role with the facilitation/synchronization role of complexin-1 and, in particular, its N-terminal domain (Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple modeling studies.

claim: A model combined the clamping role with the facilitation/synchronization role of complexin-1 and, in particular, its N-terminal domain.
source: Models of complexin function have primarily focused on a clamping or hindrance mechanism that restricts spontaneous release (Giraudo et al., 2006; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Trimbuch et al., 2014), along with a model that combined the clamping role with the facilitation/synchronization role of complexin-1 and, in particular, its N-terminal domain (Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xue et al., 2010.

claim: The different titration behaviors suggest that there are differences in mechanisms for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion and for suppressing spontaneous fusion.
source: However, if the same mechanism would facilitate synchronization as well, one would expect identical behaviors as the concentration of complexin-1 is increased. Yet, the different titration behaviors (Figure 3) suggest that there are differences in mechanisms for synchronization of Ca2+-triggered fusion and for suppressing spontaneous fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 3 showing different concentration dependencies.

claim: Genetic manipulations of the single complexin homolog in Drosophila show that the suppression and synchronization functions are genetically separable.
source: Moreover, genetic manipulations of the single complexin homolog in Drosophila show that the suppression and synchronization functions are genetically separable, also supporting the notion of distinct mechanisms in Drosophila (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cho et al., 2014.

claim: Complexin-1 and binary (syntaxin-1A/SNAP-25) SNARE complex interact weakly, as measured by a pull-down assay.
source: Complexin-1 and binary (syntaxin-1A/SNAP-25) SNARE complex interact weakly, as measured by a pull-down assay (McMahon et al., 1995) and by single molecule experiments (Weninger et al., 2008), although studies by ITC and fluorescence anisotropy did not reveal a significant interaction (Pabst et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 1995.

claim: Complexin-1 and binary (syntaxin-1A/SNAP-25) SNARE complex interact weakly, as measured by single molecule experiments.
source: Complexin-1 and binary (syntaxin-1A/SNAP-25) SNARE complex interact weakly, as measured by a pull-down assay (McMahon et al., 1995) and by single molecule experiments (Weninger et al., 2008), although studies by ITC and fluorescence anisotropy did not reveal a significant interaction (Pabst et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weninger et al., 2008.
